claim: Zebrafish dorsal forerunner cells (DFCs) originate from the superficial epithelial enveloping layer (EVL) by a process of cell ingression.
source: The zebrafish laterality organ or left-right organiser is a transient embryonic structure of epithelial nature known as Kupffer's vesicle that contains motile cilia necessary for left-right axis determination (Cooper and D'Amico, 1996; Essner et al., 2005; Kramer-Zucker et al., 2005). This organ-like epithelial structure originates from a small group of 20–30 progenitors, known as dorsal forerunner cells (DFCs), which arise at the dorsal margin of the late blastula by a process of cell ingression that converts the superficial epithelial cells of the extra-embryonic enveloping layer (EVL) into deep mesenchymal-type DFCs (Oteiza et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Oteiza et al., 2008, which describes the process of DFC formation from the EVL.

claim: DFCs move as a cell collective from their place of origin at the equator of the embryo towards the vegetal pole.
source: After ingression, DFCs move as a cell collective from their place of origin at the equator of the embryo towards the vegetal pole, reaching the terminal location for organ differentiation at the posterior tip of the notochord (Figure 1A; Figure 1—video 1; Cooper and D'Amico, 1996; Oteiza et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cooper and D'Amico, 1996 and Oteiza et al., 2008, and by reference to Figure 1A and Figure 1—video 1.

claim: DFCs are positioned ahead of the margin of the deep cell layer (DCL) during their movement.
source: On their journey, DFCs are positioned ahead of the margin of the deep cell layer (DCL), where specification signals and massive internalisation movements transform the marginal epiblast into the mesendoderm (Figure 1B; Pinheiro and Heisenberg, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pinheiro and Heisenberg, 2020, and by reference to Figure 1B.

claim: DFCs share critical determinants with the mesendoderm.
source: Despite the proximity to the DCL margin and the fact that DFCs share critical determinants with the mesendoderm (Alexander and Stainier, 1999; Warga and Kane, 2018), the movement and fate of DFCs do not appear to be affected by specification signals or mass internalisation movements of the mesendoderm, remaining separate from this cellular domain during their vegetal movement.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Alexander and Stainier, 1999 and Warga and Kane, 2018.

claim: DFCs follow the same vegetal ward direction of movement as the overlying EVL during epiboly.
source: Notably, DFCs follow the same vegetal ward direction of movement as the overlying EVL during epiboly (Bruce and Heisenberg, 2020) and appear to be physically connected to this extra-embryonic epithelial tissue, as revealed by the presence of puncta enriched in the tight junction (TJ)-associated zonula occludens one protein (ZO-1) at the DFC-EVL interface (Ablooglu et al., 2010; Oteiza et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bruce and Heisenberg, 2020, Ablooglu et al., 2010, and Oteiza et al., 2008.

claim: Puncta enriched in ZO-1 are present at the DFC-EVL interface.
source: Notably, DFCs follow the same vegetal ward direction of movement as the overlying EVL during epiboly (Bruce and Heisenberg, 2020) and appear to be physically connected to this extra-embryonic epithelial tissue, as revealed by the presence of puncta enriched in the tight junction (TJ)-associated zonula occludens one protein (ZO-1) at the DFC-EVL interface (Ablooglu et al., 2010; Oteiza et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ablooglu et al., 2010 and Oteiza et al., 2008.

claim: ZO-1 puncta mark discrete areas enriched in F-actin where DFCs contact the EVL at cell-cell junctions near the margin of the epithelium.
source: Double immunolabelling for ZO-1 and phalloidin at 75% epiboly confirmed that ZO-1 puncta marked discrete areas, also enriched in F-actin, where DFCs contacted the EVL at cell-cell junctions near the margin of the epithelium (Figure 1C – left; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunolabelling data presented in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Punctuated co-accumulation of ZO-1 and F-actin occurs at the epithelial margin where DFCs contact the YSL.
source: Also, we observed the punctuated co-accumulation of ZO-1 and F-actin at the epithelial margin where DFCs contacted the YSL (Figure 1C – right; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunolabelling data presented in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Marginal DFCs are more abundant than submarginal DFCs.
source: Indeed, the latter population of marginal DFCs was more abundant than submarginal DFCs (Figure 1D and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1D and Figure 1G.

claim: DFCs originate from dorsal EVL cells through ingression.
source: Previous work has shown that DFCs originate from dorsal EVL cells through ingression (Oteiza et al., 2008) although the underlying mechanism is currently unknown.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Oteiza et al., 2008.

claim: At early epiboly stages, EVL cells fated to become DFCs accumulate ZO-1 along their apical junctions.
source: We found that at early epiboly stages EVL cells fated to become DFCs accumulated ZO-1 along their apical junctions (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunolabelling data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: As epiboly progresses, the apical face of EVL cells fated to become DFCs gradually reduces in area to leave punctuated apical domains enriched in ZO-1 and F-actin proteins.
source: Later, as epiboly progressed, the apical face of these cells gradually reduced in area to leave punctuated apical domains enriched in ZO-1 and F-actin proteins (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunolabelling data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: DFCs arise from dorsal EVL cells by a mechanism of epithelial cell delamination mediated by apical constriction.
source: Together, these findings reveal that DFCs arise from dorsal EVL cells by a mechanism of epithelial cell delamination mediated by apical constriction.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the apical face of EVL cells fated to become DFCs gradually reduces in area, which is characteristic of apical constriction.

claim: The apical constriction process of cell delamination leaves discrete apical attachments connecting delaminating DFC progenitors with the extra-embryonic tissues.
source: Remarkably, this process leaves discrete apical attachments connecting delaminating DFC progenitors with the extra-embryonic tissues.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the apical face of EVL cells fated to become DFCs gradually reduces in area to leave punctuated apical domains enriched in ZO-1 and F-actin proteins.

claim: EVL cells fated to become DFCs gradually shrink their apical area while moving beneath the epithelial sheet.
source: We found that EVL cells fated to become DFCs gradually shrunk their apical area while moving beneath the epithelial sheet (Figure 1E and F; Figure 1—video 2), a behaviour that was specific as neighbouring dorsal EVL cells exhibited the opposite behaviour, increasing their apical area as epiboly progressed (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 1E, Figure 1F, Figure 1H, and Figure 1—video 2.

claim: Neighbouring dorsal EVL cells increase their apical area as epiboly progresses.
source: We found that EVL cells fated to become DFCs gradually shrunk their apical area while moving beneath the epithelial sheet (Figure 1E and F; Figure 1—video 2), a behaviour that was specific as neighbouring dorsal EVL cells exhibited the opposite behaviour, increasing their apical area as epiboly progressed (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 1H.

claim: The kinetics of apical area reduction varies among EVL cells fated to become DFCs.
source: Interestingly, the kinetics of apical area reduction varied among cells (Figure 1I) and resulted in discrete apical attachments that connected these cells with the YSL and EVL for extended periods (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 1I.

claim: Apical area reduction results in discrete apical attachments that connect EVL cells fated to become DFCs with the YSL and EVL for extended periods.
source: Interestingly, the kinetics of apical area reduction varied among cells (Figure 1I) and resulted in discrete apical attachments that connected these cells with the YSL and EVL for extended periods (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 1F.

claim: DFC progenitors retain long-term apical attachments with the extra-embryonic YSL and EVL as a consequence of the apical constriction process of cell delamination.
source: Collectively, these findings indicate that DFC progenitors retain long-term apical attachments with the extra-embryonic YSL and EVL as a consequence of the apical constriction process of cell delamination that gives rise to the cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that apical area reduction results in discrete apical attachments that connect EVL cells fated to become DFCs with the YSL and EVL for extended periods.

claim: Previous studies have hypothesised that the vegetal movement of DFCs relies on polarised protrusive activity.
source: However, previous studies have hypothesised that the vegetal movement of DFCs relies on polarised protrusive activity (Ablooglu et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ablooglu et al., 2010 and Zhang et al., 2016.

claim: DFCs form dynamic membrane protrusions.
source: Using in vivo imaging in an actin transgenic reporter line, we found that DFCs formed dynamic membrane protrusions (Figure 2E), as previously observed (Ablooglu et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 2E and citations to Ablooglu et al., 2010 and Zhang et al., 2016.

claim: Protrusions in DFCs are enriched at the rear (lateral and animal) edges and not at the leading (vegetal) edge of the DFC cluster.
source: However, protrusions were enriched at the rear (lateral and animal) edges and not at the leading (vegetal) edge of the DFC cluster (Figure 2A–D) arguing against a primary role of polarised cell protrusions in directing the vegetal movement of DFCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 2A–D.

claim: DFCs expressing Rac1-T17N do not form lamellar nor filopodial-like protrusions but instead show extensive membrane blebbing with no directional bias.
source: DFCs expressing Rac1-T17N did not form lamellar nor filopodial-like protrusions as in controls but instead showed extensive membrane blebbing with no directional bias (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 2F.

claim: DFCs expressing Rac1-T17N retain a persistent collective movement towards the vegetal pole.
source: Nevertheless, they still retained a persistent collective movement towards the vegetal pole (Figure 2I and K) as in controls (Figure 2H and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 2I, Figure 2K, Figure 2H, and Figure 2J.

claim: DFCs travel over 350 µm towards the vegetal pole from the time the first cell starts apical constriction until the last cells delaminate after detachment from the extra-embryonic tissues.
source: We observed that DFCs travelled over 350 µm towards the vegetal pole from the time in which the first cell started the process of apical constriction at around dome stage until the last cells delaminated after detachment from the extra-embryonic tissues at around 90% epiboly (Figure 3B – horizontal axes).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: The onset of apical constriction and the time of detachment leading to delamination are highly variable in the DFC population.
source: In agreement with the variable kinetics of apical constriction (Figure 1I), the onset of apical constriction and the time of detachment leading to delamination were also highly variable in the DFC population (Figure 3B and C – red and blue circles, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 3B and Figure 3C.

claim: The speed, direction, and extent of DFC vegetal movement tightly match the vegetal spreading of the EVL.
source: In support of this idea, the simultaneous tracking of DFCs and EVL cells revealed that the speed, direction, and extent of DFC vegetal movement tightly matched the vegetal spreading of the EVL (Figure 3D–G; Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 3D–G and Figure 3—video 1.

claim: DFCs and overlying EVL cells share the same bias in the orientation of the elongation axis.
source: Furthermore, DFCs and overlying EVL cells shared the same bias in the orientation of the elongation axis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating a morphogenetic coupling between the two tissues.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Contraction and friction-based flows of a ring-like YSL actomyosin network drive YSL/EVL vegetal spreading during epiboly.
source: Previous reports have shown that contraction and friction-based flows of a ring-like YSL actomyosin network drive YSL/EVL vegetal spreading during epiboly (Behrndt et al., 2012; Cheng et al., 2004; Heisenberg and Bellaiche, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Behrndt et al., 2012, Cheng et al., 2004, and Heisenberg and Bellaiche, 2013.

claim: Embryos expressing N-ter-MYPT1 show a speed drop in YSL/EVL vegetalward spreading.
source: Embryos expressing N-ter-MYPT1 (MYPT1) showed a speed drop in YSL/EVL vegetalward spreading. Likewise, DFCs decreased their vegetal ward speed to the same extent (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: DFCs decrease their vegetal ward speed to the same extent as YSL/EVL in embryos expressing N-ter-MYPT1.
source: Embryos expressing N-ter-MYPT1 (MYPT1) showed a speed drop in YSL/EVL vegetalward spreading. Likewise, DFCs decreased their vegetal ward speed to the same extent (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Local disruption by laser ablation of the YSL actomyosin ring in direct contact with marginal DFC apical attachments decreases the speed of EVL spreading.
source: Similarly, local disruption by laser ablation of the YSL actomyosin ring in direct contact with marginal DFC apical attachments decreased the speed of EVL spreading, as previously shown (Behrndt et al., 2012), simultaneously decreasing the speed of DFC vegetal movement near the ablated zone (Figure 4A and B; Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by laser ablation data presented in Figure 4A, Figure 4B, and Figure 4—video 1, and a citation to Behrndt et al., 2012.

claim: Local disruption by laser ablation of the YSL actomyosin ring in direct contact with marginal DFC apical attachments simultaneously decreases the speed of DFC vegetal movement near the ablated zone.
source: Similarly, local disruption by laser ablation of the YSL actomyosin ring in direct contact with marginal DFC apical attachments decreased the speed of EVL spreading, as previously shown (Behrndt et al., 2012), simultaneously decreasing the speed of DFC vegetal movement near the ablated zone (Figure 4A and B; Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by laser ablation data presented in Figure 4A, Figure 4B, and Figure 4—video 1.

claim: The progress of DFC vegetal movement requires the vegetal spreading of the extra-embryonic YSL/EVL.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that the progress of DFC vegetal movement requires the vegetal spreading of the extra-embryonic YSL/EVL.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that disrupting YSL/EVL spreading decreases DFC vegetal movement speed.

claim: Apical attachments and DFCs are under vegetally directed tension.
source: We observed that apical attachments recoiled towards the animal pole after ablation, triggering a fast retraction of the DFC body, indicating that both apical attachments and DFCs were under vegetally directed tension (Figure 4D and E; Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by laser ablation data presented in Figure 4D, Figure 4E, and Figure 4—video 2.

claim: The constricted cortical zone induced by wound repair pulls apical attachments towards the vegetal pole, restoring the vegetal directionality of DFC movement.
source: Subsequently, the constricted cortical zone induced by wound repair pulled apical attachments towards the vegetal pole, restoring the vegetal directionality of DFC movement, further indicating that apical attachments are able to transmit motion information from the EVL to DFCs (Figure 4D and E; Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by laser ablation data presented in Figure 4D, Figure 4E, and Figure 4—video 2.

claim: Isolated individual DFCs devoid of apical attachments move without persistence and directionality, even towards the animal pole in the opposite direction to the vegetal movement of the YSL/EVL.
source: In these 'natural' experiments, we observed that isolated individual DFCs devoid of apical attachments (hereafter referred to as 'detached DFCs') moved without persistence and directionality, even towards the animal pole in the opposite direction to the vegetal movement of the YSL/EVL (Figure 5B–E; Figure 4—video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 5B–E and Figure 4—video 3.

claim: Isolated individual DFCs connected with the extra-embryonic tissues by apical attachments show a persistent and directed movement toward the vegetal pole, mimicking the movement of extra-embryonic tissues.
source: In contrast, isolated individual DFCs connected with the extra-embryonic tissues by apical attachments (hereafter referred to as 'attached DFCs') showed a persistent and directed movement toward the vegetal pole, mimicking the movement of extra-embryonic tissues (Figure 5B–E; Figure 4—video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 5B–E and Figure 4—video 3.

claim: The persistence and speed of movement of DFCs correlate with the persistence and speed of movement of apical attachments.
source: Importantly, the persistence and speed of movement of DFCs correlated with the persistence and speed of movement of apical attachments (Figure 5G and H), and this close spatial and temporal relationship between apical attachments and DFC movements (Figure 5F–I) was only lost upon detachment (Figure 5E; Figure 4—video 3), indicating the requirement of physical attachment to extra-embryonic tissues for the persistent directed vegetal movement of DFCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 5G, Figure 5H, Figure 5F–I, Figure 5E, and Figure 4—video 3.

claim: Physical attachment to extra-embryonic tissues is required for the persistent directed vegetal movement of DFCs.
source: Importantly, the persistence and speed of movement of DFCs correlated with the persistence and speed of movement of apical attachments (Figure 5G and H), and this close spatial and temporal relationship between apical attachments and DFC movements (Figure 5F–I) was only lost upon detachment (Figure 5E; Figure 4—video 3), indicating the requirement of physical attachment to extra-embryonic tissues for the persistent directed vegetal movement of DFCs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the close spatial and temporal relationship between apical attachments and DFC movements is only lost upon detachment.

claim: Apical attachments are required to transmit vegetal spreading from extra-embryonic tissues to attached DFCs, guiding their vegetal movement during epiboly.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that apical attachments are required to transmit vegetal spreading from extra-embryonic tissues to attached DFCs, guiding their vegetal movement during epiboly.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that physical attachment to extra-embryonic tissues is required for the persistent directed vegetal movement of DFCs.

claim: In 55% of embryos, often one or two, and up to five detached DFCs per embryo leave the cluster as single cells.
source: We observed that in 55% of embryos, often one or two, and up to five detached DFCs per embryo left the cluster as single cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: Detached DFCs that leave the cluster move mainly in direction to the animal pole, being sequestered by the internalisation movement of the DCL and incorporating into this embryonic cell layer.
source: These cells moved mainly in direction to the animal pole, being sequestered by the internalisation movement of the DCL and incorporating into this embryonic cell layer (Figure 6B; Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 6B and Figure 6—video 1.

claim: Detached DFCs that are sequestered by the DCL mimic the morphology and movement behaviour of endodermal cells and at later stages differentiate in endodermal tissue derivatives.
source: Remarkably, this group of DFCs mimicked the morphology and movement behaviour of endodermal cells and at later stages differentiated in endodermal tissue derivatives (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DFCs transplanted into the paraxial region of host embryos follow endodermal cell fate and form endodermal tissue derivatives.
source: Furthermore, DFCs transplanted into the paraxial region of host embryos, where endodermal and mesodermal progenitors develop, also followed endodermal cell fate and form endodermal tissue derivatives (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by transplantation data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: At the onset of epiboly, the entire population of DFCs are transiting the process of delamination and thus are all attached to the YSL and EVL.
source: Immunostaining for ZO-1 and F-actin revealed that at the onset of epiboly the entire population of DFCs were transiting the process of delamination and thus were all attached to the YSL and EVL (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: As epiboly progresses, detached DFCs steadily increase to outnumber the attached DFC population from around 75% epiboly.
source: However, as epiboly progressed, detached DFCs steadily increased to outnumber the attached DFC population from around 75% epiboly, and by 90% epiboly they became the predominant pool of DFCs (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: By 90% epiboly, detached DFCs become the predominant pool of DFCs.
source: However, as epiboly progressed, detached DFCs steadily increased to outnumber the attached DFC population from around 75% epiboly, and by 90% epiboly they became the predominant pool of DFCs (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: The progressive increase of detached cells is due to DFCs completing the process of delamination and events of cell division.
source: Through time-lapse microscopy, we found that the progressive increase of detached cells was not only due to DFCs completing the process of delamination (Figure 3B), but detached DFCs also emerged from events of cell division (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data presented in Figure 3B, Figure 6D, and Figure 6E.

claim: The entire population of DFCs moves in direction to the vegetal pole in coordination with the vegetal spreading of extra-embryonic tissues until advanced stages of epiboly.
source: As previously noted, despite the continuous increase in the number of detached DFCs (Figure 6E), the entire population of DFCs still moved in direction to the vegetal pole in coordination with the vegetal spreading of extra-embryonic tissues until advanced stages of epiboly (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data presented in Figure 6E and Figure 6F.

claim: Around 85–90% of epiboly, when the percentage of detached cells reaches 80%, the DFC cluster detaches from the EVL and significantly lowers its vegetal movement.
source: Only around 85–90% of epiboly, when the percentage of detached cells reached 80%, the DFC cluster detached from the EVL and significantly lowered its vegetal movement (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data presented in Figure 6E and Figure 6F.

claim: DFCs change from being a collection of dispersed progenitors to a tightly packed cellular cluster during epiboly.
source: During epiboly, DFCs change from being a collection of dispersed progenitors to a tightly packed cellular cluster (Figure 1A; Figure 1—video 1; Oteiza et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 1A and Figure 1—video 1, and a citation to Oteiza et al., 2008.

claim: DFC clustering is achieved by progressively decreasing the distance between progenitors and increasing the contact with the surrounding cells.
source: Quantitative assessment of collective cell behaviour revealed that DFC clustering was achieved by progressively decreasing the distance between progenitors and increasing the contact with the surrounding cells (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 7A and Figure 7B.

claim: DFCs express e-cadherin mRNA.
source: During this process, DFCs express e-cadherin mRNA (Kane et al., 2005) and also localise E-cad at the cell membrane (Figure 7E), and previous reports have shown that functional abrogation of this adhesion molecule affects the cluster cohesion of DFCs leading to a scattered organisation of DFCs at 90% of epiboly (Oteiza et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kane et al., 2005 and immunostaining data presented in Figure 7E.

claim: DFCs localise E-cadherin at the cell membrane.
source: During this process, DFCs express e-cadherin mRNA (Kane et al., 2005) and also localise E-cad at the cell membrane (Figure 7E), and previous reports have shown that functional abrogation of this adhesion molecule affects the cluster cohesion of DFCs leading to a scattered organisation of DFCs at 90% of epiboly (Oteiza et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 7E.

claim: Functional abrogation of E-cadherin affects the cluster cohesion of DFCs leading to a scattered organisation of DFCs at 90% of epiboly.
source: During this process, DFCs express e-cadherin mRNA (Kane et al., 2005) and also localise E-cad at the cell membrane (Figure 7E), and previous reports have shown that functional abrogation of this adhesion molecule affects the cluster cohesion of DFCs leading to a scattered organisation of DFCs at 90% of epiboly (Oteiza et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Oteiza et al., 2010.

claim: E-cadherin knockdown disrupts cluster cohesion, leading to multiple racemes of DFCs that move in the vegetal direction guided by their apical attachments with the YSL and EVL.
source: We found that E-cad knockdown disrupted cluster cohesion, leading to multiple racemes of DFCs that moved in the vegetal direction guided by their apical attachments with the YSL and EVL (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data presented in Figure 7F.

claim: The number of detached cells exiting the DFC group towards the DCL increases significantly in E-cadherin knockdown embryos.
source: Remarkably, the number of detached cells exiting the DFC group towards the DCL increased significantly in these embryos (Figure 7G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 7G and Figure 7H.

claim: E-cadherin-mediated DFC-DFC adhesion is necessary for the recruitment of detached DFCs into the vegetal motion of attached DFCs, avoiding cell escape and promoting the formation of a tight cellular cluster.
source: These results indicate that E-cad-mediated DFC-DFC adhesion is necessary for the recruitment of detached DFCs into the vegetal motion of attached DFCs, avoiding cell escape and promoting the formation of a tight cellular cluster.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that E-cadherin knockdown disrupts cluster cohesion and increases the number of detached cells exiting the DFC group.

claim: In 57% of embryos, the DFC population organises as a single cell cluster from early stages of vegetal movement.
source: We observed that the DFC population organised as a single cell cluster from early stages of vegetal movement in 57% of embryos (Figure 8A and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridisation data presented in Figure 8A and Figure 8C.

claim: In 43% of embryos, DFCs initially form two (28%) or three (15%) small cell clusters separated by an average distance of 50 µm, which only at later stages of epiboly coalesce to form a single cluster.
source: However, in the remaining 43% of embryos, DFCs initially formed two (28%) or three (15%) small cell clusters separated by an average distance of 50 µm, which only at later stages of epiboly coalesced to form a single cluster (Figure 8B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridisation data presented in Figure 8B–D.

claim: DFCs located at the edges of distant cell clusters initiate adhesive contacts by sending out long polarised protrusions that result in the establishment of long-term adhesion between cells, allowing DFC clustering.
source: Our time-lapse image analysis revealed that DFCs located at the edges of distant cell clusters initiated adhesive contacts by sending out long polarised protrusions that resulted in the establishment of long-term adhesion between cells, allowing DFC clustering (Figure 8E; Figure 8—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data presented in Figure 8E and Figure 8—video 1.

claim: The protrusions involved in DFC clustering differ from other protrusions formed by DFCs by their longer length, increased lifetime, and alignment between clusters.
source: The protrusions involved in this process differed from other protrusions formed by DFCs not only by their longer length, but also by their increased lifetime and alignment between clusters (Figure 8F–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 8F–I.

claim: Long-range cell-cell contact interactions mediated by polarised protrusions function as seeds for the establishment of stable adhesion between DFCs.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that long-range cell-cell contact interactions mediated by polarised protrusions function as seeds for the establishment of stable adhesion between DFCs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that DFCs located at the edges of distant cell clusters initiate adhesive contacts by sending out long polarised protrusions.

claim: Subsets of small clusters of DFCs that contain several cells with apical attachments begin to detach from extra-embryonic tissues only after initiating protrusion-mediated adhesive contacts with the central cluster of attached DFCs.
source: Remarkably, using transgenic embryos expressing a fluorescent biosensor for F-actin only in DFCs, we observed a temporal connection between the formation of protrusion-mediated adhesive contacts and the loss of apical attachments. Subsets of small clusters of DFCs that contained several cells with apical attachments began to detach from extra-embryonic tissues only after initiating protrusion-mediated adhesive contacts with the central cluster of attached DFCs (Figure 8J – 0–16 min; Figure 8—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data presented in Figure 8J and Figure 8—video 2.

claim: Small clusters of DFCs complete the delamination process when fully integrated into the central DFC cluster.
source: Subsequently, they completed the delamination process when fully integrated into the central DFC cluster (Figure 8J – 23–47 min; Figure 8—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data presented in Figure 8J and Figure 8—video 2.

claim: Cell-cell contact interactions between DFCs integrate detached cells into the vegetal movement of attached cells to guide the clustering and directional vegetal movement of the entire DFC collective.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that cell-cell contact interactions between DFCs integrate detached cells into the vegetal movement of attached cells to guide the clustering and directional vegetal movement of the entire DFC collective.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that small clusters of DFCs begin to detach from extra-embryonic tissues only after initiating protrusion-mediated adhesive contacts with the central cluster of attached DFCs.

claim: Incomplete delamination serves as a cellular platform for coordinated tissue movements during development.
source: Thus, we reveal that incomplete delamination serves as a cellular platform for coordinated tissue movements during development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that apical attachments derived from incomplete delamination guide the vegetal movement of DFCs.

claim: The apical constriction process underlying the delamination of DFC progenitors follows a temporal progression that allows these cells to retain long-term apical attachments with the EVL and YSL as they spread towards the vegetal pole during epiboly.
source: Remarkably, the apical constriction process underlying the delamination of DFC progenitors follows a temporal progression that allows these cells to retain long-term apical attachments with the EVL and YSL as they spread towards the vegetal pole during epiboly.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the kinetics of apical area reduction varies among cells and results in discrete apical attachments that connect these cells with the YSL and EVL for extended periods.

claim: Apical attachments work as tissue connectors that couple DFCs with the vegetal spreading of extra-embryonic tissues, guiding their motion towards the site of differentiation at the vegetal pole.
source: Apical attachments work as tissue connectors that couple DFCs with the vegetal spreading of extra-embryonic tissues, guiding their motion towards the site of differentiation at the vegetal pole.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that apical attachments are required to transmit vegetal spreading from extra-embryonic tissues to attached DFCs.

claim: Mechanical drag by extra-embryonic tissue movement provides the critical guidance cues for DFC directed locomotion.
source: In contrast with previous hypotheses indicating that autonomous motility (Ablooglu et al., 2010) and contact-mediated repulsive interactions with the marginal DCL (Zhang et al., 2016) drive DFC vegetal movement, we show that mechanical drag by extra-embryonic tissue movement provides the critical guidance cues for DFC directed locomotion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that apical attachments are required to transmit vegetal spreading from extra-embryonic tissues to attached DFCs, and is contrasted with previous hypotheses.

claim: Incomplete delamination serves as a generic mechanism for coordinated tissue movement during development, driving the allocation of newly formed mesenchymal cell groups.
source: Here, we show that besides this canonical function, incomplete delamination serves as a generic mechanism for coordinated tissue movement during development, driving the allocation of newly formed mesenchymal cell groups.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that incomplete delamination allows DFCs to coordinate their movement with adjacent extra-embryonic tissues.

claim: Asynchrony in apical constriction generates two distinct populations of progenitors: one holding apical attachments and being pulled by the vegetal movement of extra-embryonic tissues, and a second population of detached delaminated DFCs that follows the vegetal movement of apically attached DFCs through DFC-DFC contact mechanisms.
source: Apical attachments guiding DFC movement arise from a process of apical constriction that is asynchronous among DFCs. We show that such asynchrony generates two distinct populations of progenitors, one holding apical attachments and being pulled by the vegetal movement of extra-embryonic tissues, and a second population of detached delaminated DFCs that follows the vegetal movement of apically attached DFCs through DFC-DFC contact mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the onset of apical constriction and the time of detachment leading to delamination are highly variable in the DFC population.

claim: Having an asynchronous process of cell delamination potentially increases the chances of maintaining a minimal number of apically attached DFCs able to carry the detached DFC population along their movements.
source: In the context of these evolving two populations, having an asynchronous process of cell delamination potentially increases the chances of maintaining a minimal number of apically attached DFCs able to carry the detached DFC population along their movements, a factor that becomes relevant as epiboly progresses and the ratio of attached/detached DFCs decreases.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the potential benefit of asynchronous delamination.

claim: Having asynchrony in a collective process of apical constriction promotes the even dissipation of mechanical stress over time and space, protecting the integrity of the epithelium.
source: Furthermore, as apical constriction imposes mechanical stress along the epithelial plane (Heer and Martin, 2017; Martin and Goldstein, 2014), we can speculate that having asynchrony in a collective process of apical constriction promotes the even dissipation of mechanical stress over time and space, protecting the integrity of the epithelium.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the potential benefit of asynchronous apical constriction, supported by citations to Heer and Martin, 2017 and Martin and Goldstein, 2014.

claim: Delaminated DFCs are intrinsically motile and can move towards the DCL, being sequestered by the massive internalisation movements of this embryonic cellular domain during gastrulation.
source: Delaminated DFCs are intrinsically motile and can move towards the DCL, being sequestered by the massive internalisation movements of this embryonic cellular domain during gastrulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data showing detached DFCs moving towards the DCL.

claim: When DFCs reach the DCL, either during normal development or after transplantation, they follow the endodermal path revealing that DFCs have a previously unrecognised potential to become endoderm that is expressed if they enter the developmental field of the endoderm.
source: Importantly, when DFCs reach the DCL, either during normal development or after transplantation, they follow the endodermal path revealing that DFCs have a previously unrecognised potential to become endoderm that is expressed if they enter the developmental field of the endoderm.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging and transplantation data showing DFCs differentiating into endodermal tissue derivatives.

claim: DFCs transiting the process of delamination avoid endodermal fate by establishing E-cadherin-mediated adhesive contacts with the sub-population of attached DFCs before completing the process of delamination.
source: Here, we show that DFCs transiting the process of delamination avoid endodermal fate by establishing E-cad-mediated adhesive contacts with the sub-population of attached DFCs before completing the process of delamination.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that small clusters of DFCs begin to detach from extra-embryonic tissues only after initiating protrusion-mediated adhesive contacts with the central cluster of attached DFCs.

claim: DFC-DFC contact interactions mediated by E-cadherin play a dual function: to protect delaminated cells from escaping towards the endoderm and to ensure they move together with the attached DFC population as a collective group.
source: Thus, DFC-DFC contact interactions mediated by E-cad play a dual function, to protect delaminated cells from escaping towards the endoderm and to ensure they move together with the attached DFC population as a collective group.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that E-cadherin knockdown increases the number of detached cells exiting the DFC group towards the DCL.

claim: DFCs located at long distances establish adhesive contacts by sending long polarised protrusions whose persistence and directionality differ from the other short-lived random protrusions formed by most DFCs.
source: Importantly, DFCs located at long distances establish adhesive contacts by sending long polarised protrusions whose persistence and directionality differ from the other short-lived random protrusions formed by most DFCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data showing that long inter-cluster protrusions differ in length, lifetime, and alignment from other protrusions.

claim: Migrasomes containing the chemokine ligands Cxcl12a/b become enriched in the extracellular space surrounding DFCs.
source: Notably, recent work shows that migrasomes containing the chemokine ligands Cxcl12a/b become enriched in the extracellular space surrounding DFCs (Jiang et al., 2019), thus opening the possibility that long polarised protrusions are a manifestation of a chemoattraction mechanism mediated by these guidance molecules.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2019.

claim: Long polarised protrusions may be a manifestation of a chemoattraction mechanism mediated by Cxcl12a/b guidance molecules.
source: Notably, recent work shows that migrasomes containing the chemokine ligands Cxcl12a/b become enriched in the extracellular space surrounding DFCs (Jiang et al., 2019), thus opening the possibility that long polarised protrusions are a manifestation of a chemoattraction mechanism mediated by these guidance molecules.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the potential mechanism underlying long polarised protrusions, supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2019.

claim: Small sub-groups of DFCs delaminate only after establishing adhesive contacts with the main DFC cluster, suggesting a mechanistic coupling between cell adhesion, cell motility, and the process of delamination.
source: It is also remarkable the observation that small sub-groups of DFCs delaminate only after establishing adhesive contacts with the main DFC cluster suggesting a mechanistic coupling between cell adhesion, cell motility, and the process of delamination.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that small clusters of DFCs begin to detach from extra-embryonic tissues only after initiating protrusion-mediated adhesive contacts with the central cluster of attached DFCs.

claim: E-cadherin mediates the transfer of movement information between two distinct populations of progenitor cells defined by their state in the delamination process: attached (transiting delamination) and detached (delaminated).
source: Together, these findings provide a novel developmental function for E-cad, mediating the transfer of movement information between two distinct populations of progenitor cells defined by their state in the delamination process: attached (transiting delamination) and detached (delaminated).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that E-cadherin-mediated DFC-DFC adhesion is necessary for the recruitment of detached DFCs into the vegetal motion of attached DFCs.

claim: Motion transfer from attached to detached DFCs resembles the leader-to-follower motion transmission observed in events of collective cell locomotion, many of which also require cadherin-dependent cell-cell contact interactions.
source: Remarkably, motion transfer from attached to detached DFCs resembles the leader-to-follower motion transmission observed in events of collective cell locomotion, many of which also require cadherin-dependent cell-cell contact interactions (Friedl and Gilmour, 2009; Reig et al., 2014; Theveneau and Mayor, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Friedl and Gilmour, 2009, Reig et al., 2014, and Theveneau and Mayor, 2013.

claim: The role of E-cadherin in motion transmission complements the previously described function in clusterisation.
source: In the case of DFCs, the role of E-cad in motion transmission complements the previously described function in clusterisation (Hong and Dawid, 2009; Matsui et al., 2011; Oteiza et al., 2010), and together ensure that progenitors reach the site of terminal differentiation in a sufficient number and organised as a tight collective, a prerequisite to proceed into further stages of organogenesis (Oteiza et al., 2010; Oteiza et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hong and Dawid, 2009, Matsui et al., 2011, Oteiza et al., 2010, and Oteiza et al., 2008.

claim: The proposed mechanism of DFC leader-to-follower locomotion works until the percentage of attached cells falls below the 20% limit, around 85–90% of epiboly.
source: It is worth mentioning that the proposed mechanism of DFC leader-to-follower locomotion works until the percentage of attached cells falls below the 20% limit, around 85–90% of epiboly.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data showing that the DFC cluster detaches from the EVL and significantly lowers its vegetal movement when the percentage of detached cells reaches 80%.

claim: After 85–90% of epiboly, the DFC cluster loses its physical connections with the YSL and EVL and begins an internal cellular reorganisation process leading to rosette formation and organ differentiation.
source: After this stage, the DFC cluster loses its physical connections with the YSL and EVL and begins an internal cellular reorganisation process leading to rosette formation and organ differentiation (Oteiza et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Oteiza et al., 2008.

claim: During the transition after 85–90% of epiboly, the DFC cluster continues a vegetal displacement until the end of epiboly but at a slower rate and becomes covered by the DCL.
source: During this transition, the DFC cluster continues a vegetal displacement until the end of epiboly but at a slower rate and becomes covered by the DCL.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data showing that the DFC cluster continues to move vegetally after detaching from the EVL, but at a slower rate.

claim: Caenorhabditis elegans primordial germ cells internalise during gastrulation due to cohesive contacts that these cells establish with the moving ingressing endoderm.
source: Among them, Caenorhabditis elegans primordial germ cells internalise during gastrulation due to cohesive contacts that these cells establish with the moving ingressing endoderm (Chihara and Nance, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chihara and Nance, 2012.

claim: In annual killifish, the embryonic DCL spreads during epiboly as a result of adhesive contacts with the basal epithelial domain of the expanding EVL.
source: In annual killifish, the embryonic DCL spreads during epiboly as a result of adhesive contacts with the basal epithelial domain of the expanding EVL (Reig et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reig et al., 2017.

claim: In zebrafish, the vegetal spreading of the EVL during epiboly follows the autonomous movement of the YSL to which is tightly bonded at its margin by TJ complexes.
source: In zebrafish, the vegetal spreading of the EVL during epiboly follows the autonomous movement of the YSL to which is tightly bonded at its margin by TJ complexes (Behrndt et al., 2012; Betchaku and Trinkaus, 1978; Koppen et al., 2006; Schwayer et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Behrndt et al., 2012, Betchaku and Trinkaus, 1978, Koppen et al., 2006, and Schwayer et al., 2019.

claim: Mechanical drag is an emergent mechanism of cell movement whose extent and impact during embryo morphogenesis needs to be further investigated.
source: Therefore, mechanical drag is an emergent mechanism of cell movement whose extent and impact during embryo morphogenesis needs to be further investigated.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the broader implications of mechanical drag as a mechanism of cell movement.

claim: Drag-mediated locomotion is a crucial driver of organogenesis that emerges at the interface of embryonic and extra-embryonic cellular domains.
source: Here, we show that drag-mediated locomotion is a crucial driver of organogenesis that emerges at the interface of embryonic and extra-embryonic cellular domains highlighting the essential role of mechanical information from extra-embryonic tissues in driving early embryo development (Christodoulou et al., 2019; Hiramatsu et al., 2013; Reig et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that apical attachments guide the vegetal movement of DFCs, and is supported by citations to Christodoulou et al., 2019, Hiramatsu et al., 2013, and Reig et al., 2017.
